title: Book 8 — Urania, Chapter 112
paragraphs: These, I say, having answered thus and refused to give the money, were being besieged. Themistocles, not ceasing in his desire for gain, sent threatening messages to the other islands and demanded money from them through the same envoys — those he had sent earlier to the king — saying that if they did not hand over what was demanded, he would bring the Greek fleet against them to besiege and capture them. By saying this he collected great sums from the Carystians and the Parians, who, hearing that Andros was being besieged for siding with the Medes, and that Themistocles was held in more regard than any other commander, sent money out of fear. Whether any other islanders gave money I cannot say, but I think some did — not only these. Yet the Carystians got no respite from trouble on that account; the Parians, however, escaped attack by appeasing Themistocles with money. So Themistocles, taking Andros as his starting-point, was acquiring sums of money for himself from the islanders without the knowledge of the other commanders.
